rationale: I'm switching from the 19 referential channels to the 18-channel bipolar double-banana montage that clinicians use for neonatal EEG. Neonatal seizures are focal, and subtracting neighbouring electrodes removes reference noise and artefacts shared by all channels, which should make the per-channel max and median statistics pick out the seizing region more clearly. I haven't run this yet, so I don't know whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.747.

I'm adding per-neonate normalization. Each recording's features are rescaled against that neonate's own background: subtract the recording median and divide by the interquartile range (IQR), and these normalized features are added alongside the raw ones. Background amplitude and spectrum differ greatly between neonates, so the classifier should do better at spotting seizures as a rise above that neonate's own baseline than at learning one absolute threshold for everyone. The normalization uses only each recording's own unlabelled data, so it stays label-free and neonate-independent. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.747.

Neonatal seizures are rhythmic discharges, often low in amplitude, so amplitude and band-power features alone also pick up artefacts and high-amplitude background. This change adds three rhythmicity features per channel: the peak autocorrelation at lags of 0.25–2 s (computed from the band-limited power spectrum), the fraction of 0.5–30 Hz power in a narrow peak within 0.5–8 Hz, and the negative spectral entropy. Each is taken as max and median over channels, so the per-channel-then-global design picks up a focal rhythmic region. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.747.

Right now each second is classified only from its own 8 s window. Neonatal seizures last at least 10 s and build up and change over time. This change adds temporal context per recording: centred moving averages of every feature over 15 s and 61 s, plus how far each feature sits above a 5-minute rolling median. That lets the booster use sustained, evolving rhythmicity and a local "change from background" signal instead of one-off transients. The features stay label-free and are computed separately for each recording. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.771.

Line length and RMS are currently computed on the raw referential signal, so DC drift, slow movement artefacts, 50 Hz mains noise and muscle activity dominate them rather than the 0.5–8 Hz seizure discharges. This change runs a zero-phase 4th-order Butterworth band-pass (0.5–30 Hz) on each channel before computing any feature, which should give amplitude features a better signal-to-noise ratio. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.771.

This switches from one global classifier on channel max/median summaries to the per-channel design used by Temko and Tapani. Each channel-second becomes a training row holding that channel's 9 features plus the median of all channels, so the model judges each channel against the rest of the brain at that moment. Rows take the recording's seizure label, and at test time the seizure probability for a second is the max over channels before smoothing. Neonatal seizures are focal, so a detector that ignores channel position and learns from 19× more examples should localise low-amplitude rhythmic discharges better than max/median summaries, which mix features from different channels. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.7717.

The classifier is probably overfitting to individual neonates. There are about 60 training recordings, but about 280k strongly autocorrelated seconds, and sklearn's default early stopping holds out a random 10% of those seconds. That holdout is nearly identical to the training data, so it does little to stop overfitting, and the default 20-sample leaves can memorise each neonate's background. This change turns that early stopping off and uses a heavily regularised booster with a fixed number of iterations: lower learning rate, 15-leaf trees, at least 1000 samples per leaf, L2 penalty, and stopping each tree's growth early. The aim is decision rules that hold across neonates, which matters for concatenated AUROC. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.7717.

Seizures in this dataset last tens of seconds to minutes, so per-second probabilities are probably too noisy with only 10 s of smoothing. This change keeps the features and booster as they are, but picks the moving-average length from {1, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160} s using grouped 3-fold inner CV on the training fold (concatenated AUROC on out-of-fold predictions). It also replaces zero-padded edges with nearest-value edges, which no longer pulls down scores near recording boundaries. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.7717.

All current amplitude and spectral features are absolute log powers, and background amplitude differs greatly between neonates, so the booster partly learns per-neonate amplitude levels. This change adds amplitude-invariant spectral-shape features per channel, taken as max and median over channels: the relative power in each of the 4 bands, Hjorth mobility and complexity, and the 90% spectral edge frequency. Rhythmic seizure discharges shift spectral shape the same way in every neonate, so these features should carry across neonates better. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8258.

The gradient-boosted trees can split on sharp per-neonate quirks, which probably limits how well they carry across neonates. This change averages the booster's probabilities with a smooth RBF-kernel model in the spirit of Tapani's SVM: standardized features, a Nyström approximation with 500 components, and logistic regression, trained on every 4th second. The two models' errors should be fairly independent, so the average should rank seconds better across neonates. The smoothing length is still chosen by grouped inner CV, now on the ensemble's out-of-fold predictions. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8365.

Round 1 tested the bipolar montage before the rhythmicity and spectral-shape features existed, and it replaced the referential channels instead of adding to them. This change keeps all 32 referential features and adds the same 16 per-channel features, as max and median, computed on the 18-channel neonatal double-banana montage, giving 64 features in total. Bipolar derivations remove signal shared through the reference, so focal, low-amplitude rhythmic discharges from one region should stand out more. The booster can then use whichever montage separates seizures better.

I'm replacing the single chosen moving average with a second-stage stacker. It is a regularised gradient-boosting model trained on the inner-CV out-of-fold seizure probabilities. Its inputs are those probabilities smoothed at several time scales (1–480 s), a local rolling maximum, and label-free recording-level percentiles of the probability. Concatenated AUROC across neonates is hurt mostly by false-positive seconds in neonates who never seize. Telling the model how much seizure-like evidence the whole recording holds, plus the multi-scale temporal pattern, should rank seconds better across neonates than one fixed smoothing length. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.841.

Right now each montage feature is the max or median over channels, taken separately. So the booster cannot tell whether high rhythmicity, raised power and a low-frequency spectral shape all come from the same channel. A focal neonatal seizure is exactly that combination in one region, while an artefact (ECG, respiration, a single bad electrode) usually shows only part of it. This change adds, for each montage, the full 16-feature vector of the most rhythmic channel, picked by the highest autocorrelation peak plus spectral peak fraction. That lets the model check that rhythmicity and seizure-like amplitude and spectrum coincide in one place. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.841.

Background amplitude differs from neonate to neonate, and also from electrode to electrode (for example a constantly noisy or high-impedance electrode). So the current absolute "max over channels" amplitude features are often driven by one bad electrode. Round 2 normalized the summary features, which is a different approach. Here, each channel's log amplitude and band-power features are expressed relative to that same channel's median over the whole recording (a label-free per-channel background), and only then summarized. The new features are the max over channels of these background-relative values, plus the values at the most rhythmic channel, for both montages. They should capture a focal rise above that electrode's own baseline, which is what an evolving neonatal seizure looks like. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8468.

Round 14 gained +0.018 by measuring amplitude and band-power features against each channel's own recording median. This change does the same for the other 10 per-channel features: the 3 rhythmicity features (ACF peak, peak fraction, negative entropy) and the 7 spectral-shape features (relative band powers, Hjorth, spectral edge). Some electrodes look rhythmic or spectrally odd for the whole recording because of ECG, respiration or a high-impedance contact, so only a rise above that channel's own background should count as seizure evidence. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.865.

The background-normalized features are currently summarized only as the max over channels and the value at the most rhythmic channel. Both can be driven by a single bad electrode, such as a popping contact or ECG on one lead. This change adds, for each montage, the 3rd-largest normalized value across channels. That value is high only when at least 3 channels rise above their own background at once. A real neonatal seizure usually spreads to neighbouring derivations, while a single-electrode artefact affects at most 1–2 referential channels or 2 bipolar ones. This should cut false positives without losing the focal max evidence. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8724.

A neonatal seizure is a rhythmic discharge that lasts at least 10 s in the same region. Artefacts and transients in a single channel usually last only a few seconds, or jump between channels. Round 4 smoothed features that had already been pooled across channels, which mixes evidence from different channels. This change instead takes each channel's background-normalized features, smooths them over 15 s within that channel, and only then summarizes across channels. The new summaries are the max over channels plus the full vector at the channel with the highest smoothed rhythmicity, for each montage. That lets the booster reward rhythmicity and power that stay raised in the same channel. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8724.

Smoothing each channel's background-normalised features over 15 s gave +0.0067. In this dataset, seizures usually last one to several minutes, so I'm adding a second within-channel scale of 60 s. That window spans most of an evolving discharge, so a channel that stays rhythmic and raised in power over that long gives evidence that brief artefacts and short rhythmic background bursts can't. Like the 15 s scale, it is summarised as the max over channels plus the full feature vector at the channel with the most sustained rhythmicity, for both montages. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8791.

The current background-relative features subtract each channel's median but are not rescaled. The max over channels therefore favours electrodes with naturally volatile backgrounds (noisy or artefact-prone leads), and it treats quiet and noisy neonates alike. This change also divides each channel's median-subtracted features by that channel's own robust spread (MAD, 1.4826 × the median absolute deviation, floored so that flat channels can't blow up). It then adds the max over channels of these per-channel z-scores, both unsmoothed and 15 s-smoothed, for both montages. A seizure should then register as an unusual rise for that electrode and that neonate, not just a large absolute change. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8791.

The per-channel features don't say what frequency a rhythmic discharge runs at, or whether the waveform looks like a smooth oscillation or a spiky transient. That is what separates evolving 0.5–6 Hz seizure discharges from ECG at about 2–2.5 Hz, respiration, and electrode pops or movement spikes. This change adds three waveform-morphology features to every channel: the dominant frequency of the 0.5–8 Hz spectral peak, skewness and kurtosis. They go through the existing pipeline unchanged (raw, background-relative and 15 s-smoothed summaries for both montages). I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.8791.
